def section_scale() -> None:
    rule("1.  The measured cell and the tail bar")
    print(f"  d = {D_HEADS} heads, ctx = {CTX}, product point P = d*ctx/32 = {PRODUCT_POINT}")
    print(f"  recorded knees: {RECORDED}")
    for k in RECORDED:
        print(f"    {k:4d} = {Fraction(k, PRODUCT_POINT)} P")
    print(f"  tail bar tau = {TAIL_BAR}")
    check("tau is the midpoint of 160 and 224", 2 * TAIL_BAR == 160 + 224)
    check("tau = (3/4) P", 4 * TAIL_BAR == 3 * PRODUCT_POINT)
    check("low tail = (5/8) P", 8 * 160 == 5 * PRODUCT_POINT)
    check("centre  = (7/8) P", 8 * 224 == 7 * PRODUCT_POINT)
    print(f"  all-seeds speed-up at P: {speedup(PRODUCT_POINT)} = {float(speedup(PRODUCT_POINT)):.2f}x")


def section_dichotomy() -> None:
    rule("2.  The tail statistic and the pre-registered dichotomy")
    print("     x     tail count   stable   replicated   reading    bias")
    for x in PREREG:
        e = list(RECORDED) + [x]
        c = count_le(e, TAIL_BAR)
        print(f"  {x:4d}       {c}          "
              f"{str(tail_verdict(e, TAIL_BAR, 2)):5s}    {str(x <= 160):5s}       "
              f"{str(four_seed_reading(x)):7s}  {str(bias(x)):>5s}")
        check(f"threshold form of the tail count at x={x}",
              c == (2 if x <= TAIL_BAR else 1))
        check(f"dichotomy at x={x}",
              tail_verdict(e, TAIL_BAR, 2) == (x in (160, 192)))
    print("  => stable exactly on {160, 192}; seed-specific exactly on {224, 256}")


def section_one_bit() -> None:
    rule("3.  The fourth seed carries exactly one bit")
    verdicts = {x: tail_verdict(list(RECORDED) + [x], TAIL_BAR, 2) for x in PREREG}
    check("verdict constant on {160, 192}", verdicts[160] == verdicts[192])
    check("verdict constant on {224, 256}", verdicts[224] == verdicts[256])
    check("verdict differs across the pairs", verdicts[160] != verdicts[224])
    check("both verdicts attainable (informative)", set(verdicts.values()) == {True, False})
    print("  the run cannot separate 160 from 192, nor 224 from 256:")
    print("  one training cycle returns one bit.")
    print("  finer three-way reading: replicated iff x <= 160; "
          "stable-but-not-replicated iff x = 192.")


def section_centre_invariance() -> None:
    rule("4.  Both centre summaries are constant across the outcomes")
    print("     x    224 is an l1 centre?   cost at 224   median breakdown")
    for x in PREREG:
        e = list(RECORDED) + [x]
        print(f"  {x:4d}          {str(is_l1_median(e, 224)):5s}              "
              f"{l1_cost(e, 224):5d}              {breakdown_number(4, 2)}")
        check(f"224 is an l1 centre of the sample with x={x}", is_l1_median(e, 224))
        check(f"exhaustive cost check at x={x}",
              all(l1_cost(e, 224) <= l1_cost(e, t) for t in range(0, 1025)))
        check(f"median breakdown is 2 at x={x}", empirical_breakdown(e, 2) == 2)
    print("  both summaries are the SAME for x=160 (tail stable) and x=256 (not stable),")
    print("  so no function of either can reproduce the tail verdict:")
    print("  the fourth seed is diagnostic for the tail, not the centre.")


def section_breakdown_theory() -> None:
    rule("5.  Exact breakdown numbers and the parity law")
    print("  bd(n,k) = min(k, n-k+1), verified by exhaustive adversarial search:")
    print("     n   k   formula   brute force")
    for n in (3, 4, 5, 6):
        base = [256, 224, 160, 192, 208, 240][:n]
        for k in range(1, n + 1):
            f, b = breakdown_number(n, k), empirical_breakdown(base, k)
            print(f"    {n}   {k}      {f}           {b}")
            check(f"bd({n},{k})", f == b)
    print()
    print("  lower-median breakdown ceil(n/2) -- the parity plateau:")
    for n in range(1, 10):
        star = "  <-- no gain over n-1" if n % 2 == 0 and n > 1 else ""
        print(f"    n = {n}:  beta(n) = {lower_median_breakdown(n)}{star}")
    for m in range(1, 6):
        check(f"beta({2*m}) = beta({2*m-1})",
              lower_median_breakdown(2 * m) == lower_median_breakdown(2 * m - 1))
        check(f"beta({2*m+1}) > beta({2*m})",
              lower_median_breakdown(2 * m + 1) > lower_median_breakdown(2 * m))
    print("  design law: least n with median robustness r is 2r-1 (always odd):")
    for r in range(1, 6):
        least = min(n for n in range(1, 40) if r <= lower_median_breakdown(n))
        print(f"    r = {r}:  least n = {least}   (2r-1 = {2*r-1})")
        check(f"least n for r={r}", least == 2 * r - 1)


def section_verdict_fragility() -> None:
    rule("6.  Verdict robustness: the measurable bit is the fragile one")
    print("     x    verdict   count   verdict breakdown   centre breakdown")
    for x in PREREG:
        e = list(RECORDED) + [x]
        vb = verdict_breakdown(e, TAIL_BAR, 2)
        print(f"  {x:4d}     {str(tail_verdict(e, TAIL_BAR, 2)):5s}      "
              f"{count_le(e, TAIL_BAR)}            {vb}                   "
              f"{breakdown_number(4, 2)}")
        check(f"verdict breakdown formula at x={x}",
              vb == empirical_verdict_breakdown(e, TAIL_BAR, 2))
        check(f"verdict breakdown is 1 at x={x}", vb == 1)
        check(f"verdict strictly more fragile than centre at x={x}",
              vb < breakdown_number(4, 2))
    print("  one re-run overturns the verdict whichever way it points,")
    print("  while two are needed to move the centre out of the measured range.")


def section_exclusion() -> None:
    rule("7.  Confirmation versus calibration at four seeds")
    print("  bias of the four-seed central reading against the recorded centre 224:")
    for x in (128, 160, 176, 192, 200, 224, 240, 256, 320):
        conf = "confirms tail" if x <= TAIL_BAR else "refutes tail "
        print(f"    x = {x:4d}   reading = {str(four_seed_reading(x)):7s}   "
              f"bias = {str(bias(x)):>5s}   {conf}")
    check("every confirming outcome has bias >= 16 = P/16",
          all(bias(x) >= 16 for x in range(0, TAIL_BAR + 1)))
    check("bias vanishes only at x = 224",
          [x for x in range(0, 1025) if bias(x) == 0] == [224])
    check("no outcome both confirms and calibrates",
          not any(x <= TAIL_BAR and bias(x) == 0 for x in range(0, 1025)))


def section_fifth_seed() -> None:
    rule("8.  The fifth seed reconciles confirmation and calibration")
    e5 = [256, 224, 160, 192, 224]
    e5p = [256, 224, 160, 192, 160]
    print(f"  E5  = {e5}")
    check("two seeds at or below the tail bar", count_le(e5, TAIL_BAR) == 2)
    check("median rung (quota 3 of 5) is exactly 224", quota_budget(e5, 3) == 224)
    check("zero bias against the recorded centre", quota_budget(e5, 3) - 224 == 0)
    check("centre breakdown 3", empirical_breakdown(e5, 3) == 3)
    check("224 is the unique l1 centre of E5",
          [t for t in range(0, 1025) if is_l1_median(e5, t)] == [224])
    check("160 is not an l1 centre of E5", not is_l1_median(e5, 160))
    print(f"  E5' = {e5p}")
    check("verdict breakdown 2", verdict_breakdown(e5p, TAIL_BAR, 2) == 2)
    check("verdict breakdown 2 (brute force)",
          empirical_verdict_breakdown(e5p, TAIL_BAR, 2) == 2)
    check("centre breakdown 3", empirical_breakdown(e5p, 3) == 3)
    print("  no four-seed ensemble attains either combination:")
    check("no four-seed centre breakdown above 2",
          all(breakdown_number(4, k) <= 2 for k in range(1, 5)))
    check("no four-seed verdict breakdown above 1",
          all(verdict_breakdown(list(RECORDED) + [x], TAIL_BAR, 2) == 1
              for x in range(0, 1025)))
    print("  design law for the tail: with the two recorded above-bar knees fixed,")
    print("  a quota-2 verdict robust to one re-run needs m + r - 1 + |S| = 2+2-1+2 = 5 seeds.")


def section_payoff() -> None:
    rule("9.  The physical payoff")
    print("     x    majority budget (quota 2 of 4)   certified majority speed-up")
    for x in PREREG:
        e = list(RECORDED) + [x]
        b = quota_budget(e, 2)
        s = speedup(b)
        print(f"  {x:4d}              {b:4d}                       "
              f"{s} = {float(s):.2f}x")
        if x <= TAIL_BAR:
            check(f"majority budget <= tau at x={x}", b <= TAIL_BAR)
            check(f"majority speed-up >= 32/3 at x={x}", s >= Fraction(32, 3))
    print(f"  all-seeds guarantee from the product point: {speedup(PRODUCT_POINT)} = 8.00x")
    print(f"  majority guarantee if the tail is confirmed: >= {Fraction(32,3)} "
          f"= {float(Fraction(32,3)):.2f}x")
    print("  caveats (both theorems): the quota-4 certified budget has breakdown 1,")
    print("  and the majority verdict itself has verdict breakdown 1 at four seeds.")


def main() -> None:
    print("LOW-TAIL SEED-ENSEMBLE DEMONSTRATION")
    section_scale()
    section_dichotomy()
    section_one_bit()
    section_centre_invariance()
    section_breakdown_theory()
    section_verdict_fragility()
    section_exclusion()
    section_fifth_seed()
    section_payoff()
    rule("All checks passed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

algorithms.name: Exact Finite-Sample Breakdown Number of an Order Statistic, with Witness Construction
algorithms.description: Computes bd(n, k) = min(k, n-k+1), the least number of sample points an adversary must overwrite to push the k-th order statistic outside the range of the honest data, and constructs an explicit witness attack achieving it. The downward attack overwrites k coordinates with a value below the target; the upward attack overwrites n-k+1 coordinates with a value above it. Both are oblivious -- the injected value depends only on the target and the honest range, never on which coordinates were chosen -- so the bound is realised uniformly. The module also exposes the lower-median specialisation beta(n) = ceil(n/2), whose flatness across (2m-1, 2m) is the parity law, and its inverse: the least sample size with median robustness r is 2r-1, always odd. Complexity: O(1) for the number, O(n log n) for the witness (sorting to report the corrupted statistic). Role in the pipeline: it supplies the design-side robustness figure against which the data-side verdict robustness is compared, and it is the source of the negative result that a fourth seed buys nothing at any rung.
algorithms.code:
"""Exact finite-sample breakdown number of an order statistic, with a witness attack.

Given a sample of n measured knees and a quota k, returns the exact number of
sample points an adversary must overwrite to push the k-th order statistic
outside the honest range, together with an explicit corrupted sample realising
the attack.  The number is min(k, n - k + 1); the algorithm also *constructs*
the witness so the bound can be inspected rather than trusted.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Literal, Sequence


def order_statistic(sample: Sequence[int], k: int) -> int:
    """The k-th smallest value (1-indexed), i.e. the least v with
    #{i : sample[i] <= v} >= k."""
    if not 1 <= k <= len(sample):
        raise ValueError(f"quota {k} out of range for sample size {len(sample)}")
    return sorted(sample)[k - 1]


def breakdown_number(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    """bd(n, k) = min(k, n - k + 1): k corruptions drag the statistic down,
    n - k + 1 drag it up, and fewer than the smaller of the two leave it
    trapped inside the range of the honest data."""
    if not 1 <= k <= n:
        raise ValueError("quota out of range")
    return min(k, n - k + 1)


def breakdown_witness(
    sample: Sequence[int], k: int, target: int
) -> tuple[int, list[int], Literal["down", "up"]]:
    """Construct a minimal-cardinality attack driving the k-th order statistic
    past `target`.

    Returns (number of corrupted coordinates, corrupted sample, direction).
    The attack is *oblivious*: the injected value depends only on `target` and
    the honest range, never on which coordinates were chosen.
    """
    n = len(sample)
    down_cost, up_cost = k, n - k + 1
    corrupted = list(sample)
    if down_cost <= up_cost:
        c = min(target, min(sample)) - 1
        for i in range(down_cost):                     # any k coordinates work
            corrupted[i] = c
        return down_cost, corrupted, "down"
    c = max(target, max(sample)) + 1
    for i in range(up_cost):                           # any n-k+1 coordinates
        corrupted[i] = c
    return up_cost, corrupted, "up"


def lower_median_breakdown(n: int) -> int:
    """beta(n) = ceil(n/2): the breakdown number of the lower median, and the
    maximum of bd(n, k) over all quotas k.  Flat across (2m-1, 2m) -- the
    parity law that makes even sample sizes non-optimal."""
    return (n + 1) // 2


def least_seeds_for_centre_robustness(r: int) -> int:
    """Inverse design law: the least sample size whose median tolerates r
    corrupted seeds is 2r - 1 (always odd)."""
    if r < 1:
        raise ValueError("robustness level must be at least 1")
    return 2 * r - 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    knees = [256, 224, 160, 192]
    for quota in range(1, len(knees) + 1):
        m, bad, direction = breakdown_witness(knees, quota, target=0)
        print(f"k={quota}: bd={breakdown_number(len(knees), quota)} "
              f"witness uses {m} seeds ({direction}), "
              f"corrupted statistic = {order_statistic(bad, quota)}")
    print("parity plateau:", [lower_median_breakdown(n) for n in range(1, 10)])
    print("least n for robustness r:",
          {r: least_seeds_for_centre_robustness(r) for r in range(1, 6)})

algorithms.name: Quota-Verdict Evaluation, Exact Slack-Based Breakdown, and the Tail Design Law
algorithms.description: Evaluates a tail verdict 'at least m of the seeds have knee at or below the bar tau', computes its exact breakdown number -- count - m + 1 when the verdict holds and m - count when it fails, i.e. precisely the observed slack -- and constructs a minimal flip witness. The witness moves seeds across the bar and no further (to tau+1 to destroy a true verdict, to tau to create a false one), which shows the attack is minimal in magnitude as well as in cardinality and therefore realistic: an adversary need only nudge borderline runs. The final routine inverts the relation into the design law: an ensemble whose quota-m verdict tolerates r corruptions needs a tail population of at least m + r - 1, and since seeds recorded above the bar form a disjoint population of size s, the ensemble needs at least m + r - 1 + s runs. Complexity: O(n) per evaluation, O(n) per witness. Role in the pipeline: it supplies the data-side robustness figure, exhibiting the fragility inversion (verdict breakdown 1 versus centre breakdown 2 at four seeds) and the concrete prediction that five runs are required.
algorithms.code:
"""Tail-verdict evaluation, exact verdict breakdown number, and the seed-count
design law for a pre-registered quota verdict.

A tail verdict is the threshold statement "at least m of the seeds have knee at
or below the bar tau".  Unlike the breakdown number of an order statistic --- a
design quantity fixed by (n, k) --- the breakdown number of a verdict is the
observed slack, so it must be earned by observations that actually land in the
tail.  This module evaluates the verdict, its exact breakdown number, and
inverts the relation into the minimum ensemble size needed for a prescribed
robustness.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Sequence


def count_le(sample: Sequence[int], w: int) -> int:
    """The counting primitive: number of seeds at or below w."""
    return sum(1 for k in sample if k <= w)


def tail_verdict(sample: Sequence[int], tau: int, m: int) -> bool:
    """The verdict: at least m seeds at or below the bar tau."""
    return m <= count_le(sample, tau)


def verdict_breakdown(sample: Sequence[int], tau: int, m: int) -> int:
    """Exact number of seeds an adversary must re-run to flip the verdict:
    count - m + 1 when the verdict holds, m - count when it fails."""
    c = count_le(sample, tau)
    return c - m + 1 if m <= c else m - c


def verdict_flip_witness(sample: Sequence[int], tau: int, m: int) -> list[int]:
    """A minimal corruption flipping the verdict.  Seeds are moved across the
    bar and no further: to tau + 1 to destroy a true verdict, to tau to create
    a false one."""
    corrupted = list(sample)
    if tail_verdict(sample, tau, m):
        to_move = count_le(sample, tau) - m + 1
        for i, v in enumerate(corrupted):
            if to_move and v <= tau:
                corrupted[i], to_move = tau + 1, to_move - 1
    else:
        to_move = m - count_le(sample, tau)
        for i, v in enumerate(corrupted):
            if to_move and v > tau:
                corrupted[i], to_move = tau, to_move - 1
    return corrupted


def seeds_needed_for_tail_robustness(m: int, r: int, above_bar: int) -> int:
    """Design law.  An ensemble whose quota-m tail verdict tolerates r
    corrupted seeds needs a tail population of at least m + r - 1; adding the
    `above_bar` seeds already recorded strictly above the bar --- a disjoint
    population --- gives the minimum ensemble size m + r - 1 + above_bar."""
    if m < 1 or r < 1 or above_bar < 0:
        raise ValueError("m, r must be >= 1 and above_bar >= 0")
    return m + r - 1 + above_bar


if __name__ == "__main__":
    recorded, tau, quota = [256, 224, 160], 192, 2
    for x in (160, 192, 224, 256):
        ens = recorded + [x]
        print(f"x={x:4d}  verdict={tail_verdict(ens, tau, quota)!s:5s} "
              f"count={count_le(ens, tau)} "
              f"breakdown={verdict_breakdown(ens, tau, quota)} "
              f"flip witness={verdict_flip_witness(ens, tau, quota)}")
    print("seeds needed for a majority verdict robust to one re-run:",
          seeds_needed_for_tail_robustness(m=2, r=2, above_bar=2))

algorithms.name: Counting Characterisation of the One-Dimensional Fermat-Weber Centre Set
algorithms.description: Decides whether a candidate budget minimises the total distance C(t) = sum |t - K_i| to a sample, using the counting criterion: t is a minimiser exactly when at least half the sample lies weakly at or below t and at least half lies weakly at or above it. The test requires no sortedness hypothesis, no restriction on the sample size and no assumption that the minimiser is a sample value, and it also returns the entire centre set as the closed interval between the two middle order statistics. Complexity: O(n) per candidate test, O(n log n) for the whole centre set. Role in the pipeline: it is the source of the invariance result -- the recorded centre 224 satisfies the criterion for every possible fourth seed, since it always has two sample points weakly on each side of it -- and it exhibits the parity phenomenon on the geometric side: the centre set is a nondegenerate interval at even sample sizes and a single point at odd ones.

algorithms.name: Pre-Registration Planner: Classifying Summaries as Informative or Vacuous Before the Run
algorithms.description: Given the already-recorded knees, a pre-registered outcome set, a tail bar and a quota, the planner instantiates the ensemble for each announced outcome, evaluates every summary the experiment might report (tail verdict, tail count, Fermat-Weber optimality of the recorded centre, median breakdown number, central reading) and classifies each as INFORMATIVE when its value varies across outcomes and VACUOUS when it does not. A vacuous summary is one the planned run provably cannot inform: its value is determined before the run. The planner then reports the parity verdict for the ensemble size and the minimum seed counts demanded by the centre design law (2r-1) and the tail design law (m + r - 1 + s). Complexity: O(|outcomes| * n log n) -- negligible beside a training run, which is the point: the analysis costs nothing and can veto the run. Role in the pipeline: it mechanises the central negative result, reproducing on the measured cell the finding that both centre summaries are vacuous while the tail verdict is informative with exactly two distinguishable values.

visualizations.name: The Outcome Ladder and the Confirmation/Calibration Trade-Off
visualizations.description: Two panels. Left: the three recorded knees on the budget axis with their readings on the product-point scale (P, 7/8 P, 5/8 P), the tail bar tau = 192 = (3/4)P drawn as the midpoint of the recorded tail and centre, and the four pre-registered fourth-seed outcomes coloured by verdict -- making visible that the verdict is a pure threshold in the new knee. Right: the bias of the four-seed central reading against the recorded centre 224, as a function of the fourth knee, with the confirming region shaded and the floor 16 = P/16 marked; the unique zero-bias outcome x = 224 sits outside the confirming region, which is the exclusion theorem in one picture.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualisation: the outcome ladder, the tail bar, and the confirmation /
calibration trade-off of the fourth seed.

Left panel: the three recorded knees (256, 224, 160) on the budget axis, the
tail bar tau = 192 = (3/4)P, and the four pre-registered outcomes coloured by
verdict.  Right panel: the bias of the four-seed central reading against the
recorded centre 224, as a function of the fourth knee, with the confirming
region shaded --- showing that the bias never drops below 16 = P/16 there, while
the only zero-bias outcome (224) lies outside it.

Requires matplotlib.  Writes low_tail_ladder.png.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

RECORDED: list[int] = [256, 224, 160]
TAU: int = 192
P: int = 256
PREREG: list[int] = [160, 192, 224, 256]


def central_reading(x: int) -> Fraction:
    s = sorted(RECORDED + [x])
    return Fraction(s[1] + s[2], 2)


def bias(x: int) -> float:
    return float(abs(central_reading(x) - 224))


def main() -> None:
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))

    # --- Left: the ladder -------------------------------------------------
    for k in RECORDED:
        ax1.plot([k], [1.0], "o", ms=13, color="#1f3b73", zorder=3)
        ax1.annotate(f"{k} = {Fraction(k, P)}P", (k, 1.0),
                     textcoords="offset points", xytext=(0, 16),
                     ha="center", fontsize=10, color="#1f3b73")
    ax1.axvline(TAU, color="#b3402f", lw=2, ls="--")
    ax1.annotate(r"tail bar $\tau = 192 = \frac{3}{4}P$", (TAU, 1.75),
                 ha="center", color="#b3402f", fontsize=11)
    ax1.axvspan(120, TAU, color="#b3402f", alpha=0.07)

    for x in PREREG:
        stable = x <= TAU
        ax1.plot([x], [0.4], "s", ms=12,
                 color="#2c7a4b" if stable else "#8a8a8a", zorder=3)
        ax1.annotate("stable" if stable else "seed-specific", (x, 0.4),
                     textcoords="offset points", xytext=(0, -22), ha="center",
                     fontsize=9, color="#2c7a4b" if stable else "#6a6a6a")
    ax1.annotate("recorded knees", (124, 1.32), fontsize=10, color="#1f3b73")
    ax1.annotate("pre-registered\nfourth-seed outcomes", (124, 0.68),
                 fontsize=10, color="#444")
    ax1.set_xlim(120, 300)
    ax1.set_ylim(0.0, 2.1)
    ax1.set_yticks([])
    ax1.set_xlabel("retained attention budget (knee)")
    ax1.set_title("One bar, one bit: the low-tail experiment")

    # --- Right: bias profile ---------------------------------------------
    xs = list(range(130, 301))
    ax2.plot(xs, [bias(x) for x in xs], lw=2.2, color="#1f3b73")
    ax2.axvspan(130, TAU, color="#2c7a4b", alpha=0.10)
    ax2.axhline(16, color="#b3402f", lw=1.5, ls=":")
    ax2.annotate(r"bias floor $16 = P/16$", (250, 17.2),
                 color="#b3402f", fontsize=10)
    ax2.annotate("outcomes confirming\nthe low tail", (140, 27),
                 color="#2c7a4b", fontsize=10)
    ax2.plot([224], [0], "o", ms=10, color="#2c7a4b")
    ax2.annotate("only calibrating outcome\n(refutes the tail)", (224, 1.5),
                 textcoords="offset points", xytext=(12, 26), fontsize=10)
    ax2.set_xlabel("fourth knee $x$")
    ax2.set_ylabel("bias of the four-seed central reading")
    ax2.set_title("Confirmation and calibration are exclusive at four seeds")
    ax2.set_ylim(-2, 36)

    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("low_tail_ladder.png", dpi=170)
    print("wrote low_tail_ladder.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

visualizations.name: The Parity Staircase: Why Even Sample Sizes Are Never Optima
visualizations.description: Two panels. Left: the tent function bd(n,k) = min(k, n-k+1) plotted against the quota k for several sample sizes, showing that no rung is more robust than the lower median and that the four-seed tent peaks at the same height as the three-seed one. Right: the peak value beta(n) = ceil(n/2) plotted against n as a staircase, flat across every pair (2m-1, 2m); each tread is a sample size at which one more run buys no robustness, each riser a size at which a run pays. The three-, four- and five-seed designs of the experiment are marked on the staircase.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualisation: the parity staircase.

Left panel: the exact breakdown number bd(n, k) = min(k, n-k+1) of the k-th
order statistic, as a tent function of the quota k, for several sample sizes n;
its peak is the lower median.  Right panel: that peak, beta(n) = ceil(n/2),
plotted against n --- a staircase that is flat across every pair (2m-1, 2m).
Each flat tread is a sample size at which one more run buys no robustness; the
riser is where a run pays.  The three/four/five-seed designs of the low-tail
experiment are marked.

Requires matplotlib.  Writes parity_staircase.png.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def breakdown_number(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    return min(k, n - k + 1)


def lower_median_breakdown(n: int) -> int:
    return (n + 1) // 2


def main() -> None:
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))

    for n, colour in zip((3, 4, 5, 8), ("#1f3b73", "#b3402f", "#2c7a4b", "#8a6d1f")):
        ks = list(range(1, n + 1))
        ax1.plot(ks, [breakdown_number(n, k) for k in ks], "o-", lw=2,
                 color=colour, label=f"n = {n}")
    ax1.set_xlabel("quota $k$ (which order statistic is reported)")
    ax1.set_ylabel("breakdown number $\\min(k,\\,n-k+1)$")
    ax1.set_title("No rung beats the lower median")
    ax1.legend()
    ax1.grid(alpha=0.25)

    ns = list(range(1, 13))
    ax2.step(ns, [lower_median_breakdown(n) for n in ns], where="post", lw=2.4,
             color="#1f3b73")
    for n in ns:
        ax2.plot([n], [lower_median_breakdown(n)], "o", ms=6, color="#1f3b73")
    for n, label, colour, offset in ((3, "3 seeds\n(current)", "#2c7a4b", (-52, 2)),
                                     (4, "4 seeds\n(no gain)", "#b3402f", (-16, -40)),
                                     (5, "5 seeds\n(gain)", "#2c7a4b", (-8, 14))):
        ax2.annotate(label, (n, lower_median_breakdown(n)),
                     textcoords="offset points", xytext=offset,
                     fontsize=10, color=colour)
    ax2.set_xlabel("number of seeds $n$")
    ax2.set_ylabel(r"$\beta(n)=\lceil n/2\rceil$")
    ax2.set_title("The parity staircase: even sizes are never optima")
    ax2.grid(alpha=0.25)
    ax2.set_xticks(ns)

    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("parity_staircase.png", dpi=170)
    print("wrote parity_staircase.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

visualizations.name: Centre Invariance: Total-Distance Curves Across Every Pre-Registered Outcome
visualizations.description: Five panels showing the piecewise-linear total-distance cost C(t) = sum |t - K_i| of the ensemble against the candidate centre t: one for each pre-registered fourth-seed outcome, plus the five-seed reconciling ensemble. In each panel the minimising segment -- the full Fermat-Weber centre set -- is shaded and the recorded centre 224 is marked. The recorded centre lies in the minimising segment of every four-seed panel, which is why no function of the centre can encode the tail verdict; and the five-seed panel's centre set collapses to the single point 224, showing how the odd sample breaks the tie that the even one leaves open.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualisation: why the centre cannot move.

For each pre-registered fourth-seed outcome, the piecewise-linear total-distance
cost C(t) = sum_i |t - K_i| of the four-seed ensemble is plotted against the
candidate budget t, with the flat minimising segment (the Fermat-Weber centre
set) highlighted.  In every case the recorded centre 224 lies in that segment:
the fourth seed cannot dislodge it, whatever it reports.  The fifth panel shows
the five-seed reconciling ensemble, whose centre set collapses to the single
point 224.

Requires matplotlib.  Writes centre_invariance.png.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

RECORDED: list[int] = [256, 224, 160]
PREREG: list[int] = [160, 192, 224, 256]
FIVE: list[int] = [256, 224, 160, 192, 224]


def cost(sample: list[int], t: int) -> int:
    return sum(abs(t - k) for k in sample)


def centre_interval(sample: list[int]) -> tuple[int, int]:
    s = sorted(sample)
    n = len(s)
    return s[(n - 1) // 2], s[n // 2]


def main() -> None:
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(18, 4), sharey=False)
    panels = [(f"fourth seed $x = {x}$", RECORDED + [x]) for x in PREREG]
    panels.append(("five seeds $\\{256,224,160,192,224\\}$", FIVE))

    ts = list(range(120, 301))
    for ax, (title, sample) in zip(axes, panels):
        ax.plot(ts, [cost(sample, t) for t in ts], lw=2, color="#1f3b73")
        lo, hi = centre_interval(sample)
        ax.axvspan(lo, hi, color="#2c7a4b", alpha=0.20)
        ax.plot([224], [cost(sample, 224)], "o", ms=9, color="#b3402f")
        ax.annotate("224", (224, cost(sample, 224)),
                    textcoords="offset points", xytext=(6, 10),
                    color="#b3402f", fontsize=10)
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11)
        ax.set_xlabel("candidate centre $t$")
        ax.grid(alpha=0.2)
    axes[0].set_ylabel("total distance $C(t)=\\sum_i |t-K_i|$")

    fig.suptitle("The recorded centre 224 minimises the total distance for every outcome "
                 "(shaded: the full centre set)", fontsize=12)
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.93))
    fig.savefig("centre_invariance.png", dpi=170)
    print("wrote centre_invariance.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Why the centre never moves — click for the argument

A value t minimises the total distance C(t) = Σ|t − Ki| exactly when at least half the sample lies weakly at or below t and at least half lies weakly at or above it. Move right by δ: the points at or below t each cost you δ more, the others save at most δ, so the net change is at least δ(2·#{Ki ≤ t} − n) ≥ 0. Mirror the argument to move left.

For the four-seed sample {256, 224, 160, x}, the value 224 always has two points weakly below it (224 and 160) and two weakly above it (224 and 256), whatever x is — and with n = 4 the condition asks only for two on each side. Hence 224 is a centre for every possible fourth seed: the run cannot inform the centre, because the answer is fixed before the run.

Why the verdict is so fragile — click for the argument

A verdict “at least m seeds at or below τ” is flipped by moving seeds across the bar. If it currently holds with count c, an adversary must push c − m + 1 tail seeds just above τ; if it fails, they must pull m − c seeds down to τ. That number is the exact verdict breakdown number, and it equals the observed slack.

At four seeds the count is 2 (verdict holds, slack 0) or 1 (verdict fails, deficit 1), so the breakdown number is 1 either way. Compare the centre, whose breakdown number is 2. The bit the experiment can measure is strictly less robust than the bit it cannot — because centre robustness is a property of the design, while verdict robustness is slack that must be bought with runs that actually land in the tail.

The two design laws, derived

Centre. Dragging the k-th smallest value below any bound takes k corrupted runs (overwrite k coordinates with a very small number); dragging it above any bound takes n − k + 1. Fewer than the smaller of the two, and a counting argument traps the estimate inside the honest range. So bd(n,k) = min(k, n−k+1), maximised at k = ⌈n/2⌉ with value ⌈n/2⌉. Inverting: r ≤ ⌈n/2⌉ ⟺ 2r − 1 ≤ n, so the least ensemble with robustness r has 2r − 1 runs — always odd. Padding an odd design to the next even size buys nothing at any quota.

Tail. A verdict “at least m seeds at or below the bar” holding with count c survives exactly c − m corruptions and dies at c − m + 1. So robustness r needs a tail population of at least m + r − 1. Seeds already recorded above the bar are a disjoint population, so if s of them exist, the ensemble needs at least m + r − 1 + s runs.

The measured cell. With the recorded knees 256 and 224 permanently above the bar (s = 2), a majority verdict (m = 2) robust to one re-run (r = 2) needs 2 + 2 − 1 + 2 = 5 runs. The centre law independently demands 5 for robustness 3. The fourth run is diagnostic; the fifth is decisive.

# One Bar, One Bit: What a Single Extra Training Run Can Decide

*A guided tour of the low-tail experiment — from a practical question about attention budgets to
an exact arithmetic of experiment design.*

---

## 1. The setting: where is the cliff?

Attention costs $O(n^2)$ in the context length. The standard economy is to keep only the top $k$
attention entries per query and mask the rest, which buys a speed-up of roughly $\mathrm{ctx}/k$
— provided you stay above the **knee**:

$$K \;=\; \min\{k \;:\; \text{accuracy at budget } k \;\ge\; 0.98 \times \text{accuracy at full budget}\}.$$

Below the knee the model breaks; above it, you are paying for attention you did not need. Knees are
measured, not derived, and they depend on the training seed. In the configuration studied here — a
small causal transformer, $d = 4$ heads, context $\mathrm{ctx} = 2048$, accuracy bar $0.98$ — three
seeds gave three different knees:

$$K = \{256,\; 224,\; 160\}.$$

The cell has a natural reference scale, the **product point** $P = d\cdot\mathrm{ctx}/32 = 256$, which
is exactly an $8\times$ speed-up. So the three knees read $P$, $\tfrac78 P$ and $\tfrac58 P$. The
middle value $224 = \tfrac78 P$ is the **centre**; the straggler $160 = \tfrac58 P$ is the **low tail**.

> **The question.** Is that low tail a real feature of the configuration — worth roughly $13\times$
> instead of $8\times$ — or an accident of one seed? Run a fourth seed. But *what exactly* can the
> fourth run decide?

---

## 2. Play first: the fourth seed laboratory

Before any theory, get your hands on the object. Drag the fourth seed's knee and watch eight
summaries update at once. Two of them will refuse to move no matter what you do — that refusal is
the main theorem of this work.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

<details>
<summary>Things to try (and what they show)</summary>

- **Sweep $x$ from 128 to 320.** The verdict flips exactly once, at $x = 192$. It is a *threshold*
  functional: one bit, no more.
- **Compare $x = 160$ and $x = 192$.** Identical verdict. The run cannot tell a repeat of the recorded
  tail from the intermediate rung.
- **Watch "Is 224 still a centre?"** It never changes. Nor does the centre robustness number.
- **Find the zero-bias outcome.** It is $x = 224$ — which is also an outcome that *refutes* the tail.
  At four seeds you may confirm or calibrate, never both.
- **Tick "add a fifth seed"**, set $x = 192$, $y = 224$. Now the tail is stable, the reading is exactly
  $224$, and centre robustness jumps to $3$.
</details>

---

## 3. One bar, one bit

Pre-registration means naming the outcomes and their verdicts before the run. The pre-registered
outcome set was $\{160, 192, 224, 256\}$, with the declared reading: $\{160,192\}$ establishes the low
tail; $\{224,256\}$ marks it seed-specific.

Where does the dividing line come from? The natural separator between the measured tail $\tfrac58P$
and the measured centre $\tfrac78P$ is their midpoint, the **tail bar**

$$\tau \;=\; \frac{160+224}{2} \;=\; 192 \;=\; \tfrac34 P .$$

Call a seed a *tail seed* if its knee is at or below $\tau$, and call the tail **stable** if at least
two of the four seeds are tail seeds — a tail with a witness, not a singleton. Of the recorded knees
only $160$ qualifies, so

$$\#\{\text{tail seeds}\} \;=\; \begin{cases}2, & x \le 192,\\ 1, & x > 192,\end{cases}$$

which reproduces the pre-registered dichotomy exactly.

> **Theorem (the experiment, as pre-registered).** On the announced outcome set, the low tail is
> stable if and only if the fourth knee lies in $\{160, 192\}$.
>
> **Theorem (exactly one bit).** The verdict is constant on $\{160,192\}$, constant on
> $\{224,256\}$, and differs across the pairs; both verdicts are attainable. A full training run
> returns a single yes/no.

{{visualization:0}}

---

## 4. What the run *cannot* see

Two standard summaries describe the centre of a knee sample.

**The Fermat–Weber point** minimises total distance $C(t) = \sum_i |t - K_i|$ — the robust "middle".
It has a clean counting characterisation.

> **Theorem (counting characterisation of the $\ell^1$ centre).** A value $t$ minimises
> $\sum_i|t-K_i|$ over an $n$-point sample if and only if at least half the sample lies weakly at or
> below $t$ and at least half lies weakly at or above it.

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal the two-line proof</summary>

Move right from $t$ by $\delta > 0$. Every sample point at or below $t$ costs you exactly $\delta$
more; every other point saves at most $\delta$. So the net change is at least
$\delta\,(2\,\#\{K_i \le t\} - n) \ge 0$ under the hypothesis. Mirror the argument for moving left,
using $\#\{K_i \ge t\}$. Conversely, if fewer than half the points lie at or below $t$, the cost is
affine with negative slope up to the next sample value, which is therefore strictly better.
</details>

Apply it: for the sample $\{256, 224, 160, x\}$ the value $224$ always has two points weakly below
(itself and $160$) and two weakly above (itself and $256$) — and with $n = 4$ two on each side is all
the condition asks. So **$224$ is a Fermat–Weber centre for every possible fourth seed.**

{{visualization:2}}

**The breakdown number** is the other summary: the least number of runs an adversary must replace,
with arbitrary values, to push the estimate outside the honest range.

> **Theorem (exact finite-sample breakdown number).** For the $k$-th smallest value of an
> $n$-point sample, $\mathrm{bd}(n,k) = \min\{k,\; n-k+1\}$.

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal the proof sketch</summary>

*Attacks.* Overwrite $k$ coordinates with a value far below everything: the $k$-th smallest is now
that value, arbitrarily low. Overwrite $n-k+1$ coordinates with a value far above everything: below
it the count never reaches $k$, so the $k$-th smallest is that value, arbitrarily high. Both attacks
are *oblivious* — they never look at the honest data.

*Stability.* If $m < k$ and $k+m \le n$ coordinates are corrupted, the counting function moves by at
most $m$ at every argument, so quota $k$ is still not met below the honest minimum and is already met
at the honest maximum. The estimate is trapped inside the honest range.
</details>

Since the median breakdown number of any four-seed sample is $2$ — the same as three seeds — **both
centre summaries are constant across all four pre-registered outcomes**. And a constant cannot
predict something that varies:

> **Theorem (diagnostic for the tail, not the centre).** No function of the statement "$224$ is a
> centre", and no function of the median breakdown number, reproduces the tail verdict on the
> pre-registered outcome set. The tail bit is logically independent of everything the centre records.

You can verify this classification mechanically, before spending the run:

{{algorithm:3}}

---

## 5. The parity law: why *four* is the wrong number

Maximise $\mathrm{bd}(n,k) = \min\{k, n-k+1\}$ over $k$: the best rung is the lower median, with value
$\lceil n/2\rceil$. And $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ is flat across $(2m-1, 2m)$:

$$\lceil 3/2\rceil = \lceil 4/2 \rceil = 2, \qquad \lceil 5/2 \rceil = 3.$$

Three seeds tolerate one bad run. Four seeds tolerate one bad run. Five tolerate two. Inverting:
**the least ensemble whose median tolerates $r$ corrupted runs has $2r-1$ members — always odd.**
An even sample size is never a design optimum for any robustness target.

{{visualization:1}}

Explore the two design laws — the centre law and the tail law — and see exactly how many runs each
target costs:

{{interactive_demo:1}}

{{algorithm:0}}

---

## 6. Confirming and calibrating pull in opposite directions

With four measurements the conventional central reading is the midpoint of the two middle values.
Write $b(x)$ for its distance from the recorded centre $224$:

$$b(x) = \begin{cases} 32, & x \le 160,\\ \tfrac12(224-x), & 160 \le x \le 224,\\
\tfrac12(x-224), & 224 \le x \le 256,\\ 16, & x \ge 256.\end{cases}$$

It vanishes only at $x = 224$ — an outcome that refutes the tail. Conversely every confirming outcome
has $x \le 192$, hence $b(x) \ge \tfrac12(224-192) = 16 = P/16$.

> **Theorem (exclusion).** No four-seed outcome both confirms the low tail and calibrates the centre.
> Every confirming outcome biases the central reading by at least $P/16$.
>
> **Theorem (the fifth seed reconciles).** The ensemble $\{256,224,160,192,224\}$ has two seeds at or
> below the tail bar, reads its median rung *exactly* at $224 = \tfrac78P$, and has breakdown number
> $3$ — the first two impossible together at four seeds, the third impossible at four seeds at any
> rung.

---

## 7. The twist: the measurable bit is the fragile one

We measured how robust the centre is. How robust is the *verdict*?

> **Theorem (exact verdict breakdown number).** A verdict "at least $m$ seeds at or below $\tau$"
> that holds with count $c$ is overturned by exactly $c - m + 1$ re-runs; one that fails is created by
> exactly $m - c$ re-runs.

At four seeds, $m = 2$ and $c \in \{1,2\}$, so the verdict breakdown number is $1$ **either way**. One
unlucky re-run overturns whatever the experiment concludes — while the centre it cannot influence has
breakdown $2$. Centre robustness is a *design* quantity, fixed by $n$; verdict robustness is *slack*,
which must be bought with runs that actually land in the tail.

{{algorithm:1}}

<details>
<summary>Why moving seeds "just across the bar" is the optimal attack</summary>

The verdict depends on the sample only through the count $\#\{i : K_i \le \tau\}$. To change the
count by one you need only move a single seed from one side of $\tau$ to the other; magnitude beyond
that is wasted. So minimal attacks move seeds to $\tau$ (to create a verdict) or to $\tau + 1$ (to
destroy one), and the number of moves required is exactly the slack. This also shows the attack is
*realistic*: an adversary need not fabricate absurd numbers, only nudge borderline runs — and the
recorded low-tail seed cleared the accuracy bar by $0.001$.
</details>

---

## 8. The centre, computed

The whole centre set — not just one minimiser — falls out of the counting characterisation in
$O(n\log n)$:

{{algorithm:2}}

At four seeds with $x = 160$ the centre set is the whole interval $[160, 224]$: both the recorded
centre and the low tail minimise total distance, and the sample cannot choose between them. At five
seeds the tie breaks and $224$ becomes the unique centre. Non-uniqueness at even sizes is the same
parity phenomenon once more.

---

## 9. What it is worth

If the fourth seed confirms the low tail, the majority budget of the cell is at most
$\tfrac34 P = 192$, so the speed-up certified for a majority of seeds is at least

$$\frac{2048}{192} = \frac{32}{3} \approx 10.7\times,$$

against the $8\times$ that the product point guarantees for all seeds. Two caveats, both theorems: the
all-seeds certified budget has breakdown number $1$, and the majority verdict itself has verdict
breakdown $1$ at four seeds.

Run the complete numerical verification of every claim on this page:

{{demo:0}}

---

## 10. The moral

Experiment design is usually argued in the language of statistics. A surprising amount of it is
decided earlier, at the level of counting. The centre and the tail are two quotas of one counting
function $w \mapsto \#\{i : K_i \le w\}$ — the verdict reads it at a fixed bar, the centre at a moving
one. Once that is visible, the design facts are arithmetic:

- even sample sizes are never robustness optima, because $\lceil n/2\rceil$ is flat across $(2m-1,2m)$;
- a summary constant across all pre-registered outcomes cannot be informed by the run;
- confirming a tail and calibrating a centre are quotas an even sample pulls apart;
- verdict robustness is slack, and slack must be bought with observations in the tail.

None of it depends on a distributional model. Before you spend the next training run, it is worth
knowing which of your questions it is arithmetically capable of answering.

**Further reading.** The classical background is the
[Fermat–Weber problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_median) (the geometric median, whose
one-dimensional case is the median itself), the
[breakdown point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robust_statistics#Breakdown_point) of robust
statistics, [order statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_statistic), and
[pre-registration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preregistration_(science)) as a discipline for
fixing verdicts before data arrive. On the systems side, the practical motivation is
[sparse attention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attention_(machine_learning)) and top-$k$ truncation
of the attention matrix.
